title: Pull request and code review workflow
description: Learn about Pull request and code review workflow. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Pull requests and code review are the primary quality gates for most engineering teams. A well-structured workflow catches bugs early, spreads knowledge, and ensures the main branch remains stable.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers writing effective PR descriptions, review best practices, approval workflows, CI integration, and etiquette for asynchronous code reviews.
The Anatomy of a Good Pull Request
A good pull request is small, focused, and well-described. Aim for under 400 lines of code changed when possible. Large PRs are harder to review thoroughly and more likely to contain defects.

items: Title: short, imperative, describes the outcome
Description: explains why the change is needed
Scope: links to the issue or design document
Testing: steps to verify the change
Screenshots or recordings for UI changes

data.title: Pull Request Title and Description
data.code:
Title: feat(dashboard): add export to CSV

Description:
Add CSV export to the analytics dashboard so users can download reports.

Closes #892

## Testing
1. Navigate to /dashboard/analytics
2. Click Export CSV
3. Verify file downloads with correct headers

data.text: Small Pull Requests
Small pull requests get faster, more thorough reviews. If a feature requires many files, split it into sequential PRs. Each PR should deliver a single, testable increment of value.

items: Target 200-400 lines of code changed
One logical change per PR
Split large features into incremental PRs
Avoid mixing refactors with features in the same PR

data.title: The 400-Line Rule
data.text: Studies show review defect detection drops significantly after 400 lines. If your PR exceeds that, ask whether it can be split.
Branch Protection Rules
Branch protection prevents direct pushes to important branches. Require pull request reviews, passing CI checks, and signed commits where applicable.

rows: Ensures approval is based on current code
Applies rules to everyone, including leads
Prevents history rewriting on shared branches

data.text: CI Checks
Continuous Integration runs automated tests, linters, and security scanners on every pull request. If any check fails, the PR cannot be merged.

items: Lint and typecheck run on every push
Unit and integration tests run in CI
Security scanners flag vulnerable dependencies
Coverage reports are posted as PR comments
Preview deployments let reviewers try the change

data.title: GitHub Actions CI Workflow
data.code:
name: CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test -- --coverage

data.text: Review Best Practices
Good reviews are specific, kind, and focused on the code rather than the author. Reviewers should explain the reasoning behind suggestions and prioritize issues by severity.

items: Start with a high-level summary before diving into details
Ask questions instead of making demands
Flag security, performance, and correctness issues first
Praise good solutions and thoughtful design
Suggest, do not command

data.title: Review the Intent First
data.text: Before checking line-by-line, understand what the author is trying to achieve. A small diff with a flawed approach may need more discussion than a large diff with a solid design.
Review Etiquette

items: Respond to review comments within one business day
Mark conversations as resolved when addressed
Do not merge your own PR without at least one approval
Avoid nitpicking style if a linter handles it
Keep tone neutral and professional

data.title: Constructive Review Comment
data.code: Suggestion: Consider using `Array.map` here instead of a for loop. It is more idiomatic and easier to test. If performance is critical, we can benchmark both.

data.text: Requesting Changes vs Commenting

GitHub and GitLab distinguish between comments and change requests. Use request changes when the PR cannot be merged until the issue is fixed. Use comments for suggestions that the author may accept or decline.

cards.title: Approve
cards.description: The PR meets standards and can be merged.

cards.title: Request Changes
cards.description: Block merge until the author addresses the issue.

data.text: Addressing Review Feedback
When reviewers leave feedback, push new commits to the same branch. Do not create a new pull request unless the branch was deleted. Respond to each comment to show you have considered the feedback.

data.title: Responding to Review Feedback
data.code:
# In the PR comment thread
> Please handle the error case here.

Done. Added a try-catch block in commit def5678.

data.text: CODEOWNERS
The CODEOWNERS file automatically requests reviews from specific individuals or teams when files in certain paths are changed. This ensures the right people are notified without manual assignment.

data.title: CODEOWNERS File
data.code:
# Default owners for everything
* @team/platform

# Authentication files require auth team review
/src/auth/ @team/auth

# Database migrations require DBA review
/prisma/migrations/ @team/dba

data.text: Merge Strategies in Pull Requests
GitHub offers three merge methods: create a merge commit, squash and merge, or rebase and merge. Each produces a different main-branch history.

cards.title: Create merge commit
cards.description: Preserves full branch history with merge commits.

cards.title: Squash and merge
cards.description: Collapses all commits into one on main.

data.text: Self-Review
Before requesting reviews, review your own pull request. Read the diff as if you were a teammate. Fix typos, remove debug logs, and ensure the PR description is accurate.

items: Read every changed file in the GitHub UI
Remove commented-out code and console.log statements
Verify the PR description matches the actual changes
Run the app locally and test the affected flows

data.text: Review Checklists

data.title: Code Review Checklist
items: Does the code solve the stated problem?
Are there edge cases or error paths not handled?
Is the code readable and maintainable?
Are tests added or updated appropriately?
Does the change follow existing patterns?
Are there performance or security concerns?
Is the documentation updated?

data.text: Asynchronous Reviews
Most code reviews happen asynchronously across time zones. Be explicit about deadlines and expectations.

items: State expected review turnaround time in the PR
Use GitHub notifications or Slack for urgent reviews
Document review expectations in the team handbook
Respect focus time: do not expect instant responses

data.text: Large Refactoring Pull Requests
Refactoring PRs that touch many files need extra care. Pair with a senior engineer, break the refactor into small PRs, and ensure tests pass after each step.

data.title: No Refactor-and-Feature Mix
data.text: A PR that refactors half the codebase and adds a new feature is almost impossible to review. Split them into separate PRs.
Reviewing Tests
Review tests with the same rigor as production code. A test suite full of weak assertions gives a false sense of security.

items: Tests should cover new behavior and regression scenarios
Avoid asserting implementation details that may change
Check for skipped or disabled tests
Ensure tests are deterministic and do not depend on execution order

data.text: Security in Code Review
Code review is a critical security control. Look for hardcoded secrets, SQL injection vectors, unsafe deserialization, improper access checks, and missing input validation.

data.title: Common Security Review Items

data.text: Performance Considerations
Reviewers should flag N+1 queries, unnecessary re-renders, large bundle additions, and inefficient algorithms.

items: Check for N+1 queries in database access code
Verify that lists use virtualization when large
Watch for synchronous loops on the main thread
Consider the bundle size impact of new dependencies

data.text: Advanced Review Practices
These practices round out the workflow: templates and draft PRs, automation, and the harder human parts of review such as constructive feedback and approvals.
PR Templates
A PR template guides authors to include all necessary information. Store templates in .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md or .gitlab/merge_request_templates/.

<optional>

data.text: Multiple PR Templates
GitHub supports multiple PR templates. Authors can choose the appropriate template from a dropdown. Use different templates for features, bug fixes, and dependencies.
Draft Pull Requests
Draft PRs signal work-in-progress. Reviewers can leave early feedback without the pressure of a final review. Mark the PR as ready when it is reviewable.

items: Use draft PRs for early design feedback
Mark as ready only when tests pass
Do not merge draft PRs without final review
Add a WIP label for extra clarity

data.text: Review Request Best Practices
When requesting a review, tag specific people rather than entire teams. Explain what you want them to focus on: security, performance, architecture, or style.

data.title: Review Request Message
data.code: @alice Please review the security implications of this change. Specifically, I want to make sure the new endpoint properly validates the JWT claims.

data.text: Automated Code Review
Tools like Danger, Reviewdog, and Lintly can automate parts of code review. They post comments on PRs when conventions are violated, freeing human reviewers to focus on logic and design.

data.title: Danger JS Configuration

data.text: Constructive Feedback
Frame feedback as suggestions, not demands. Explain the reasoning behind your suggestions. A comment like 'Consider using map for clarity' is more helpful than 'Use map here.'
Handling Disagreements
If you disagree with a review comment, discuss it respectfully. If you cannot reach agreement, involve a tech lead or architect. Do not let disagreements stall the PR indefinitely.

items: Reply with your reasoning and evidence
Reference documentation or previous decisions
Involve a third party if needed
Escalate to tech lead if the decision has broader impact

data.text: Approval Workflows
Define clear approval requirements. Some teams require one approval from any teammate. Others require approval from a specific domain expert. Document the rules in your CONTRIBUTING guide.

rows: Require domain expert for complex areas

data.text: Required Reviewers
GitHub and GitLab let you require specific reviewers for certain paths. This ensures critical code always gets reviewed by the right person.

items: Require DBA review for migrations
Require security team review for auth changes
Require accessibility review for UI components
Automate reviewer assignment with GitHub Actions

data.text: Summary

Effective pull request workflows combine clear descriptions, automated checks, thoughtful review, and consistent team conventions. The goal is to ship high-quality code while maintaining team velocity and morale.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Write a clear description explaining the why
Use branch protection and CI as quality gates
Squash or rebase before merge based on team convention
